papers.title: Calibrating demand models versus adjusting OD matrices with traffic counts: a controlled comparison
papers.abstract: Traffic counts are routinely used to calibrate travel demand models, particularly when the origin-destination (OD) matrix is not observed directly. An important modelling decision is whether to adjust individual OD flows or the parameters of the demand model that generates them. The latter approach uses fewer parameters and preserves a relationship between zonal characteristics and demand, but its accuracy depends on the assumed model structure. We compare three established approaches using the same prior information, traffic counts and equilibrium assignment. They estimate five production-gravity coefficients, origin and destination adjustment factors, or individual OD flows. Synthetic experiments on the Eastern Massachusetts and Chicago Sketch networks allow recovery to be assessed against known demand under different forms of model misspecification. Calibrating the five-coefficient model gives better OD recovery and held-out link-flow prediction when demand follows its assumptions or a two-purpose gravity process. Its advantage declines or reverses when destination choice or production relationships vary across zones. Cellwise adjustment achieves the closest fit to calibration counts in 65 of 66 evaluated conditions, yet it recovers OD demand least accurately of the three approaches in 45 of them. These findings show that model parameterisation matters beyond calibration fit. For transport planning, traffic counts should be used alongside independent evidence on trip production and distribution when selecting and validating a demand model.

papers.title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
papers.abstract: Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

papers.title: Replication Certification at Publication: Checkable by Anyone, Anywhere, in Seconds, Forever
papers.abstract: Authors increasingly deposit replication datasets---the data and code behind publications---in archives, and journals increasingly require them to, under progressively onerous rules. But a deposit alone proves little, so authors keep paying: months for the journal's reanalyses, years answering readers' questions, and rancor as failed replications become accusations because no record establishes what actually ran. We introduce a replication certificate: a cryptographically signed record of the deposited files and logged output. It replaces the journal's reanalyses with evidence anyone can check in seconds, which no one, including the archive, can backdate, and no one can fake without risking detection. Certification asks little of anyone and benefits everyone: The author deposits, then reruns the analysis once under a random seed the archive computes from the deposit's hash and a blockchain block; the archive signs, timestamps (in that blockchain), and stores the record---confidential data included---without rerunning anything; the journal merely checks a website for the certificate; and anyone can check or replay any step decades later.

papers.title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions
papers.abstract: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

papers.title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness
papers.abstract: Clinical notes contain rich patient information, such as diagnoses or medications, making them valuable for patient representation learning. Recent advances in large language models have further improved the ability to extract meaningful representations from clinical texts. However, clinical notes are often missing. For example, in our MIMIC-IV cohort, 35.15% of patients have no eligible discharge summaries. In such cases, representations can be learned from other modalities such as structured data, chest X-rays, or radiology reports. Yet the availability of these modalities is influenced by clinical decision-making and varies across patients, potentially producing modality missing-not-at-random (MMNAR) patterns. We propose a causal representation learning framework that leverages observed data and informative missingness in multimodal clinical records. It consists of: (1) an MMNAR-aware modality fusion component that integrates structured data, imaging, and text while conditioning on missingness patterns to capture patient health and clinician-driven assignment; (2) a modality reconstruction component with latent alignment to preserve modality information in the learned representation; and (3) a multitask outcome prediction model with a rectifier that corrects for residual bias from specific modality observation patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across MIMIC-IV and eICU show consistent gains over the strongest baselines, achieving relative AUC improvements of up to 4.3% for hospital readmission and 2.7% for ICU admission.

papers.title: CausalCompass: Evaluating the Robustness of Time-Series Causal Discovery in Misspecified Scenarios
papers.abstract: Causal discovery from time series is a fundamental task in machine learning. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by a reliance on untestable causal assumptions and by the lack of robustness-oriented evaluation in existing benchmarks. To address these challenges, we propose CausalCompass, a flexible and extensible benchmark framework designed to assess the robustness of time-series causal discovery (TSCD) methods under violations of modeling assumptions. To demonstrate the practical utility of CausalCompass, we conduct extensive benchmarking of representative TSCD algorithms across eight assumption-violation scenarios. Our experimental results indicate that no single method consistently attains optimal performance across all settings. Nevertheless, in most scenarios, the methods exhibiting superior overall performance are deep learning-based approaches. We further provide hyperparameter sensitivity analyses to deepen the understanding of these findings. We additionally conduct ablation experiments to explain the strong performance of deep learning-based methods under assumption violations. We also find that NTS-NOTEARS relies on standardized preprocessing in practice, performing poorly in the vanilla setting but exhibiting strong performance after standardization. Finally, our work aims to provide a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of TSCD methods under assumption violations, thereby facilitating their broader adoption in real-world applications. The user-friendly implementation, documentation and datasets are available at https://github.com/huiyang-yi/CausalCompass.

papers.title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
papers.abstract: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.

papers.title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
papers.abstract: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

papers.title: Hypergraph Generation via Structured Stochastic Diffusion
papers.abstract: Hypergraphs model higher-order interactions, but realistic hypergraph generation remains difficult because incidence, hyperedge-size heterogeneity, and overlap structure are not faithfully captured by pairwise reductions. We propose \HEDGE, a generative model defined directly on relaxed incidence matrices via a structured stochastic diffusion. The forward process combines a hypergraph-specific two-sided heat operator with an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck component, preserving structure-aware noising near the data while yielding an explicit Gaussian terminal law. Conditional on an observed hypergraph, this forward process is linear-Gaussian, so conditional means, covariances, scores, and reverse-drift targets are available in closed form. We therefore learn a permutation-equivariant state-only reverse-drift field in incidence space by regressing onto exact conditional targets, and generate samples by simulating a learned reverse-time SDE from the Gaussian base law. We establish exactness in the ideal state-only setting together with finite-horizon stability guarantees, and empirically show improved hypergraph generation quality relative to strong baselines.

papers.title: Self-Distillation is Optimal Among Spectral Shrinkage Estimators
papers.abstract: Self-distillation has emerged as a promising technique for improving model performance in modern machine learning systems. We develop the statistical foundations of self-distillation in high-dimensional linear regression by introducing and analyzing a broad class of estimators, namely spectral shrinkage estimators. We consider both spiked and general covariance matrices. For the former, we establish that when the covariance has $s$ distinct spikes, $s$-step self-distillation achieves optimal prediction among spectral shrinkage estimators, outperforming well-known estimators in statistics and machine learning. Moreover, we show that $s$ steps are necessary for optimality: any $(s-k)$-step distilled estimator is strictly suboptimal for $1 \leq k \leq s$. For general covariance matrices, we show that self-distillation approaches the optimal limiting prediction risk among continuous spectral shrinkage estimators as the number of distillation steps increases. We further develop a generalized cross-validation procedure for selecting the distillation parameters from data and establish an asymptotic oracle guarantee for the resulting estimator. We also study a federated approach where multiple data centers share spectral shrinkage estimators and a common server seeks to aggregate them to achieve optimal performance. In this case, we find that the best local rule again takes the form of self-distillation, though it differs from the optimal rule when data are hosted centrally on a single server. Together, our results explain why self-distillation improves predictive performance and provide a broader statistical framework that connects it to classical shrinkage-based methods.

papers.title: Guidance for Prior Change via Density Ratio Estimation
papers.abstract: Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) serves as a vital framework for parameter inference in scientific fields where simulators involve intractable likelihoods, yet while amortized generative models offer rapid posterior estimation, they are often restricted by the specific priors used during training, thereby limiting their flexibility as prior knowledge evolves. To address this prior dependency, PriorGuide was introduced as an inference-time guidance method, but due to its intractable formulation, it relies on Gaussian approximations of the reverse transition kernel and Gaussian mixture model fitting for the prior ratio, both of which introduce systematic bias. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an unbiased test-time guidance framework that leverages Density Ratio Estimation (DRE) to learn a score guidance term, effectively decoupling the inference process from the prior training. Moreover, our framework remains agnostic to the specific density ratio estimators, making it a general and flexible framework for handling prior changes. Experimental results across multiple tasks demonstrate that our method matches or outperforms PriorGuide on C2ST and MMD in most tasks while maintaining robustness even under limited overlap between the training and target priors. Furthermore, we apply our method to Bayesian updating for parameter inference from planetary light-curve data, where it also demonstrates strong effectiveness and robustness. Code is available at https://github.com/a-chenchen/dre-based-prior-guidance .

papers.title: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices
papers.abstract: We consider Box-Cox transformations of correlation matrices, $\Phi_\alpha(C)=\mathrm{vecl}\{(C^{\alpha}-I)/\alpha\}$, with Jacobian $J_\alpha$. The family nests the raw correlations at $\alpha=1$, the generalised Fisher transformation (GFT), $C\mapsto\mathrm{vecl}(\log C)$, at $\alpha=0$, and the negated off-diagonal concentration coordinates at $\alpha=-1$. The inverse problem is a strictly convex program for every $\alpha$, so every member is injective. The map is onto $\mathbb{R}^{d}$, $d=n(n-1)/2$, if and only if $\alpha\le0$, such that $\alpha=0$ defines the boundary for unrestricted parametrizations. For $\alpha>0$ the image is bounded. The conditioning obeys the bound $\kappa(J_\alpha)\le\kappa(C)^{|1-\alpha|}$, where $\kappa(C)=\lambda_{\max}(C)/\lambda_{\min}(C)$, and on the surjective range the exponent is smallest at $\alpha=0$. Under Gaussian sampling with $n\geq3$, the asymptotic covariance of the transformed sample correlations is the identity at independence for every member, but only $\alpha=0$ retains the identity to first order in the correlations, whereas the leading joint third cumulant at independence vanishes only at $\alpha=1/3$. Finally, applying the transformation to the diagonal rescaling of $C$ that makes the result hollow adds a new family to the existing correlation parametrizations. For every $\alpha$ the rescaling solves a strictly convex problem and the inverse is explicit, and the scaled coordinates are unrestricted exactly when $\alpha=0$, where they recover the known global normal coordinates, centred at independence, for the efficient information metric of the correlations.

papers.title: What is the Long-Term Value of Reliability?
papers.abstract: We describe Chronos LTV, a system to measure the long-term impact of delays and other service defects on key business metrics. We use Markov decision processes to model customer interactions over time, and formalize our target estimand as the marginal policy effect with respect to moving the average delay rate. Given this setup, we show that we can identify long-term effects under a sequential unconfoundedness assumption where delays are as good as random given observed order characteristics; and can estimate these effects using a simple covariate-balancing algorithm.

papers.title: Calibrated Order-Randomized Rosenblatt Tests
papers.abstract: We test whether a multivariate vector X conforms to a specified distribution F, as in copula modelling and density forecasting. The Rosenblatt transform reduces this to testing uniformity, but its arbitrary coordinate ordering affects power under dependence. We study order randomization: transforming under many random orderings and merging evidence with dependence-robust rules. Reordering only redistributes the Mahalanobis signal energy, so one ordering is a lucky or unlucky draw, and pooling raises calibrated power. We compare against two order-invariant baselines, the chi-squared energy test and the symmetric-root test. With F known, the e-value average over orderings is at least as powerful as the symmetric-root test in every setting we ran, and as the chi-squared test on concentrated and fully diffuse departures. With Gaussian mean and covariance estimated, the classical conditional probability integral transform keeps each ordering's p-values exact and e-values valid, a parametric bootstrap calibrates the pooled tests, and the comparisons hold except for deficits of at most 0.02 against the symmetric-root test on single-coordinate departures. Validating a Gaussian risk model for nine currencies, the test flags Brexit, COVID and other episodes; it extends to any null with computable, simulable conditionals.

papers.title: Robust Ensemble Kalman Filtering Under Observation Noise Misspecification
papers.abstract: We address observation noise misspecification in Bayesian filtering of dynamical systems via generalised Bayesian inference. Mismatch in tail decay between the true data generating process and an assumed observation model, often indicated via outliers, can strongly impact Bayesian updates in Kalman filters and their ensemble approximations. Adjusting information processing in the analysis step by employing diffusion score matching achieves robustness while maintaining closed-form Gaussian updates and good uncertainty quantification. We provide theoretical properties of this novel Kalman filter in linear Gaussian state space systems covering conjugacy of the analysis step, robustness, covariance stability, and tuning. We extend the approach to non-linear signal dynamics by adapting ensemble Kalman filter variants. Simulation studies on 2D target tracking and the Lorenz-63 and 40D Lorenz-96 systems highlight a critical trade-off between robustness and stability in filtering.

papers.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference
papers.abstract: We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over all estimators and over design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population of $\sum_i d_i$ potential outcomes, where $d_i$ is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit $i$. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are the potential outcomes, its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments, and its weights are induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class, and the unweighted hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential-outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes: joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory for average treatment effects without interference, saturation designs under partial interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.

papers.title: Supervised Factor-Augmented Matrix Regression with Weak Factors
papers.abstract: We develop a supervised factor-augmented matrix regression framework for high-dimensional analysis with weak factors. When factor loadings are concentrated on unknown subsets of rows and columns, conventional full-matrix factor extraction may suffer substantial signal dilution, with weakness in one matrix dimension propagating to estimation in the other. We characterize this two-way weak-loading phenomenon for both \(\alpha\)-PCA and projected estimators and show that their loading and factor estimates may deteriorate under weak signals. To address this problem, we propose a sequential response-guided screening procedure that identifies informative rows and columns prior to factor extraction. We establish exact support recovery and show that post-screening factor re-estimation converts the weak-loading problem into a pervasive one relative to the retained dimensions, yielding sharper convergence rates under substantially weaker dimensional growth conditions and consistent factor-number determination. We further establish asymptotic distributions for both unrestricted and bilinear regression estimators based on the estimated matrix factors. Simulations demonstrate substantial improvements in support recovery and factor estimation under weak signals. We illustrate the gains obtained by the response-guided factor construction with two empirical applications.

papers.title: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity
papers.abstract: This paper develops a general M-estimation framework for censored regression models under endogeneity. A two-stage estimation is proposed to address the issue of endogeneity in the first stage and the issue of censoring in linear regression models in the second stage. The issue of endogeneity is addressed via instrumental variables using the control function approach. The issue of censoring in linear regression models is addressed via M-estimation using a suitably defined class of loss functions yielding a class of estimators. Thus, the proposed general M-estimation framework nests several existing estimators as special cases for the respective loss functions. Moreover, this provides flexibility of accommodating a broad range of robust loss functions that have not previously been studied in the context of censored regression. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality for the proposed class of estimators. An empirical study based on simulated datasets is conducted to illustrate general M-estimation for various choices of loss functions and to examine the finite-sample performance of various resulting estimators.

papers.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
papers.abstract: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite this broad potential impact, selection bias is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct it, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle and assumptions, and we compare methods addressing the same form of selection by their assumptions, data requirements and limitations. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R, prepares input for the external SPREG software, and provides worked examples on simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection, one of which we present in full. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with recommendations for bias-aware study design, sensitivity analysis and reporting.

papers.title: Bayesian Unit-level Quantile Modeling with Application to Wealth Data
papers.abstract: Modeling wealth quantiles over time and space and across fine-grained demographic classifications is of vital importance to policy makers. However, such data present unique challenges for standard small area estimation methodologies because they are highly skewed and heavy-tailed with both positive and negative values. Traditional area-level modeling and design-based approaches struggle to capture these features. Meanwhile, existing unit-level methodology frequently treats the survey design as ignorable and does not apply to surveys that are repeated over time. Often the analysis is restricted to alternative response variables that are non-negative, such as poverty indicators or income. To overcome these limitations, we propose a Bayesian, asymmetric Laplace pseudolikelihood model that is able to capture the major features of wealth while adjusting for survey weights and accounting for both spatial and temporal dependence. We present a Gibbs sampling algorithm for our model, as well as a variational Bayes algorithm for fast computation. We apply the method to the Survey of Income and Program Participation to characterize geographic, temporal, and demographic variation in the distribution of U.S. household wealth, including for sparsely sampled domains where direct estimates are unavailable or unstable.

papers.title: Competitive Balance Beyond Standings: Bayesian Inference for Latent Tiers and Structural Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: Competitive balance has long been a central concern in sports economics, tied to outcome uncertainty, fan engagement, and the way leagues design their policies. Most existing measures of competitive balance are built from standings or winning percentages, which say little about how overall parity relates to the way teams sort into latent competitive tiers. We propose a Bayesian framework based on the Bradley-Terry model that jointly estimates the number of competitive tiers and team memberships. To capture the overall degree of competitive heterogeneity, we introduce a structural balance parameter defined on the unit interval within a hierarchical model, and we establish theoretical results giving this parameter a clear interpretation:it is directly tied to the separation between tiers, and overall heterogeneity depends on both the size and frequency of cross-tier differences. Importantly, structural balance is distinct from the information content of the schedule itself, so leagues with different numbers of teams and games can be compared on equal footing. Inference is carried out with an efficient posterior sampling algorithm that jointly handles team abilities, tier structure, home advantage, and structural balance. Simulation studies validate the proposed method, showing accurate recovery of the latent competitive structure and correct performance of the structural-balance testing procedure. Applied to the NBA and NFL, it reveals that the two leagues exhibit similar global structural balance despite very different competitive organizations: the NBA has three latent tiers, while the NFL has two broader ones, and the NFL's sparser schedule produces considerably more posterior uncertainty. Overall parity, it turns out, can mask quite different forms of competitive stratification-something standings-based measures alone cannot detect.

papers.title: Risk-set reconstruction balance: zero-targeted diagnostics for artificial censoring in clone-censor-weight analyses
papers.abstract: In clone-censor-weight (CCW) analyses, inverse probability of censoring weighting corrects selection from artificial censoring at protocol deviation. Balance diagnostics, such as the end-of-grace between-strategy standardised mean difference (SMD) and censoring balance, compare different populations, and their zero targets under a correct model are not formally stated. We show that, under positivity and a correct censoring model, the weighted retained individuals reconstruct the risk set before each censoring interval and the baseline population, and we propose risk-set reconstruction balance (RRB), which measures how far they depart from these two populations. Interval RRB has a zero target for every history function, including post-baseline covariates, for which between-strategy SMDs have none. Cumulative RRB keeps a zero target for baseline covariates after outcome events, whereas the end-of-grace SMD acquires a depletion term. In simulations, interval RRB responded to an omitted term's effect on censoring whether or not the term was prognostic. Under correct models, the exceedance rate of its studentised maximum over a null reference for chance imbalance was 3.5-6.0% (nominal 5%) when the censoring model pooled nine intervals and mostly 1.0-4.5% under censoring in a single interval. With many early events, cumulative RRB stayed near zero, whereas the end-of-grace SMD reached 0.40; under loss to follow-up that the weights ignored, cumulative RRB departed from zero and interval RRB stayed small. In a case study, interval RRB flagged a dispensing indicator outside the censoring model. Interval RRB checks the censoring model, and cumulative RRB the representation of the baseline population.

papers.title: Coherent forecast combination for linearly constrained multiple time series
papers.abstract: Forecasting linearly constrained multiple time series, as those arising in National Accounts, energy systems and supply chain planning, requires that the forecasts of all variables jointly satisfy the underlying accounting or resource-balance identities. When several experts provide forecasts for some or all of the variables, classical forecast combination operates on each variable and ignores the linear constraints, while forecast reconciliation enforces such constraints by using a single forecast per variable. To bridge this gap, we develop an original coherent forecast combination framework, in which the joint problem of combination across experts and coherence across variables is formulated as a linearly constrained optimization problem. Closed-form expressions are derived for the coherent combined forecast and its error covariance matrix, and the statistical properties of the resulting estimators are discussed. A Monte Carlo experiment and a forecasting application to an Australian daily electricity generation dataset confirm that the proposed approach significantly improves forecast accuracy with respect to standard forecast combination and reconciliation alternatives.

papers.title: Exchangeable Gaussian Processes with application to epidemics
papers.abstract: We develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling collections of related epidemic trajectories using exchangeable Gaussian processes. The proposed formulation induces structured dependence across time-varying transmission processes through shared latent Gaussian process components, leading to interpretable pooling behaviour, variance decompositions and intra-class correlation parameters that quantify information sharing across populations. The framework accommodates both direct and indirect observation regimes, including noisy measurements of effective reproduction numbers, latent transmission models for Chikungunya outbreaks and age-structured epidemic systems driven by partially observed infection dynamics. We discuss connections with broader multi-output Gaussian process formulations, including coregionalisation and latent factor models, while emphasising the interpretation of the proposed approach as a functional random-effects framework for related temporal trajectories. A simulation study investigates the behaviour of the proposed models under varying cross-population dependence structures including dependent, weakly dependent and independent settings. Across several epidemic applications, the proposed models demonstrate strong predictive performance while providing interpretable insights into shared and population-specific transmission dynamics.

papers.title: Quasi-Maximum Likelihood Estimation for a Genuinely Unbalanced Dynamic Network Panel Data Model
papers.abstract: This paper develops quasi-maximum likelihood estimation for genuinely unbalanced dynamic network panel data models. We first study a baseline one-way fixed effect specification and then extend the framework to two-way fixed effects. The model accommodates contemporaneous and lagged network spillovers, temporal dependence, and a listing effect that operates when a unit first appears in the panel. For the baseline specification, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the QMLE, characterize the incidental-parameter bias, and propose a bias-corrected estimator. We further provide a consistent estimator of the asymptotic covariance matrix, to enable feasible inference. Under the two-way fixed effect extension, we derive the corresponding asymptotic distribution, bias correction, and covariance matrix estimator, accounting for the additional bias component induced by the time fixed effects. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite sample performance of the proposed estimators and inference procedure. An empirical application to Airbnb listings from New Zealand and New York City reveals region-specific patterns in spatial and temporal price transmission, highlighting the importance of modeling genuine unbalancedness in dynamic network settings.

papers.title: Assessment of evidence against homogeneity in exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots
papers.abstract: Exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots are constructed by displaying all subgroup treatment effects of interest against subgroup sample size, providing a useful overview of the observed treatment effect heterogeneity in a clinical trial. As in any exploratory subgroup analysis, however, the observed estimates suffer from small sample sizes and multiplicity issues. To facilitate more interpretable exploratory assessments, this paper introduces a computationally efficient method to generate homogeneity regions within exhaustive subgroup treatment effect plots. Using the Doubly Robust (DR) learner, pseudo-outcomes are used to estimate subgroup effects and derive reference distributions, quantifying how surprising observed heterogeneity is under a homogeneous effects model. Explicit formulas are derived for the homogeneity region and different methods for calculation of the critical values are compared. The method is illustrated with a cardiovascular trial and evaluated via simulation, showing well-calibrated inference and improved performance over standard approaches using simple differences of observed group means.

papers.title: Competing Risk Analysis in Cardiovascular Outcome Trials: A Simulation Comparison of Cox and Fine-Gray Models
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular outcome trials commonly face competing risks when non-CV death prevents observation of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE). While Cox proportional hazards models treat competing events as independent censoring, Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard models explicitly handle competing risks, targeting different estimands. This simulation study using bivariate copula models systematically varies competing event rates (0.5%-5% annually), treatment effects on competing events (50% reduction to 50% increase), and correlation structures to compare these approaches. At competing event rates typical of CV outcome trials (~1% annually), Cox and Fine-Gray produce nearly identical hazard ratio estimates regardless of correlation strength or treatment effect direction. Substantial divergence occurs only with high competing rates and directionally discordant treatment effects, though neither estimator provides unbiased estimates of true marginal hazard ratios under these conditions. In typical CV trial settings with low competing event rates, Cox models remain appropriate for primary analysis due to superior interpretability. Pre-specified Cox models should not be abandoned for competing risk methods. Importantly, Fine-Gray models do not constitute proper sensitivity analyses to Cox models per ICH E9(R1), as they target different estimands rather than testing assumptions. As supplementary analysis, cumulative incidence using Aalen-Johansen estimator can provide transparency about competing risk impact. Under high competing-risk scenarios, alternative approaches such as inverse probability of censoring weighting, multiple imputation, or inclusion of all-cause mortality in primary endpoints warrant consideration.

papers.title: Anchors Away: Navigating Single-Arm Indirect Comparisons with Multilevel Unanchored Meta-Regression (ML-UMR-SA)
papers.abstract: Unanchored indirect treatment comparisons using single-arm evidence are increasingly used in health technology assessment (HTA) when anchored comparisons of randomized evidence are not possible. Existing population-adjusted methods, including matching-adjusted indirect comparison (MAIC) and simulated treatment comparison (STC), are generally limited to pairwise analyses and typically estimate marginal effects in the comparator study population, which may differ from the decision-relevant target population. We propose multilevel unanchored meta-regression for single-arm indirect comparisons (ML-UMR-SA), a Bayesian outcome-regression framework for synthesizing individual patient data and aggregate data from single-arm evidence. ML-UMR-SA respecifies multilevel network meta-regression to pool absolute outcomes rather than relative treatment effects, jointly modeling individual- and aggregate-level data and linking aggregate outcomes through marginalization over study-specific covariate distributions, enabling estimation across multiple treatments, studies, and target populations. ML-UMR-SA distinguishes assumptions required to identify treatment effects from those required to transport results to target populations. Valid inference relies on strong and often unverifiable assumptions, particularly conditional constancy of absolute effects and cross-treatment identifying assumptions such as the shared prognostic factor assumption (SPFA). These requirements are made explicit within a Bayesian modeling framework that facilitates sensitivity analyses. In simulations without unobserved confounding, ML-UMR-SA produced low bias and nominal coverage for comparator-population effects. Transportability to alternative populations depended critically on identifying assumptions, whereas incorporating subgroup information restored near-unbiased estimation and nominal coverage.

papers.title: Advection-aligned block Vecchia inference for spatio-temporal Gaussian processes
papers.abstract: Vecchia approximations enable scalable likelihood-based inference for large Gaussian process models, but their accuracy depends on the choice of conditioning sets. For spatio-temporal processes with advection, target-centered conditioning can omit informative past observations. Motivated by total column ozone observations from the Geostationary Environment Monitoring Spectrometer (GEMS), we propose a data-driven, advection-aligned block Vecchia approximation that incorporates estimated transport direction into temporal conditioning geometry. Observation locations need not lie on a regular grid. An initial advection vector is estimated from the data and used once to select transport-aligned past-time conditioning blocks. The resulting graph is held fixed during optimization, while covariance and advection parameters remain free to vary. This separates neighbor selection from covariance estimation, avoids repeated parameter-dependent neighbor searches, and provides an interpretable connection between conditioning geometry and estimated transport. Batched graphics processing unit (GPU) operations evaluate the likelihood and its gradients. In a matched comparison of daily GEMS datasets from July 2024 and July 2025, advection-aligned conditioning attained a lower fitted Vecchia negative log-likelihood than target-centered conditioning on 53 of 61 days. In six Mat\'ern simulation scenarios with 120 matched eight-hour fields each, advection-aligned conditioning reduced advection-vector root mean squared error relative to target-centered conditioning at the same conditioning-block budget, with the largest reduction under strong transport.

papers.title: Power improvements and exact shortcuts for closed permutation maxT testing with discrete data
papers.abstract: In permutation tests with discrete data, especially in small samples, different permutations often yield the same test statistic. The resulting ties can make the test conservative and reduce power. This conservatism can be particularly pronounced for maximum statistics: permutations may have the same maximum but differ at other endpoints, so the remaining endpoint statistics are discarded. We develop two power improvements for closed permutation maxT tests by refining the treatment of ties. The first method uses a single uniform random variable shared across all local tests in the closed testing procedure. This shared-uniform construction maximizes the rejection probability of every elementary hypothesis among all ways of coordinating the same randomized local tests. It also preserves an exact linear step-down shortcut. The second method is the deterministic two-endpoint augmentation (tea) test, which uses the second-largest endpoint statistic to resolve ties in the maximum. This additional information can favour rejection under alternatives while preserving null validity, without auxiliary randomization. Its full closure admits an exact quadratic shortcut. More generally, augmentation using any fixed number of endpoint statistics admits an exact polynomial shortcut. Both procedures retain every rejection made by classical closed maxT procedures and provide strong finite-sample control of the family-wise error rate under intersection-null permutation invariance. In simulations with sparse binary outcomes, both methods improve power over classical closed maxT testing. When many endpoints are tested, the tea test also often outperforms shared-uniform randomization.
